summary: This unit teaches you to take apart, inspect and put back together electromechanical components: single-phase motors, brush motors, contactors, relays and solenoids. You will learn to make them safe, plan and record the work, use pullers, presses and other tools correctly, judge wear on bearings, brushes, contacts and windings, and reassemble and test so that the component works as it did when new.

blocks.p: Motors, contactors and relays wear out: bearings get noisy, brushes wear down, contacts burn and windings get dirty. Many faults can be put right by taking the component apart, cleaning and inspecting it, replacing the worn parts and putting it back together correctly. This unit is for Level 2 trainees who do this work under supervision, in the workshop and on site.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Make the component safe
Unplug it, or isolate, lock off, tag and prove it dead; discharge capacitors; deal with springs, belts, pressure and heavy parts.
Plan the job
Read the service manual and exploded diagram, collect the right tools, and set out a clean bench with labelled trays.
Record before you dismantle
Copy the nameplate, photograph and label the wiring, make match marks, and note shims, washers and which way parts face.
Dismantle without damage
Use pullers, a soft-faced mallet, circlip pliers and the right keys and spanners; never hammer shafts, bearings or castings.
Clean and inspect the parts
Judge bearings, shafts, windings, brushes, commutators, centrifugal switches, capacitors, contacts and springs, and write down what you find.
Replace worn parts
Fit bearings, brushes, contact kits and capacitors of the correct type and rating, the correct way.
Reassemble in the right order
Work in the reverse order, line up the match marks, tighten evenly, and check that the shaft or armature moves freely.
Test and hand back
Carry out the dead tests, have the instructor do the run test, refit all guards, and complete the job card.

blocks.h: Where you will meet this work in Jamaica

ul: **Water pumps** on tanks and wells, **pool pumps** at hotels and villas, and **pressure pumps** in homes, which run long hours and often suffer from damp and heat.
**Fans**: ceiling, pedestal and exhaust fans, and the fan motors in air-conditioners.
**Workshop machines**: table saws in furniture shops, bench grinders, compressors, mixers in bakeries, and the portable drills and grinders used on every site.
**Control gear**: contactors and relays in motor starters, gate motors, water-heater and pump controls.

blocks.note: Equipment near the coast suffers from salt air, which rusts bearings, frames and terminals and corrodes contacts. Expect more corrosion on motors and panels in seaside towns, and look for it when you inspect.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Read the sections in order: they follow a real job, from making it safe to handing it back. Then try the practice test and read every explanation. Your instructor will show you the Centre's motors, tools and test bench.
An electromechanical component turns electrical energy into movement, or uses movement to switch electricity. You will take apart these kinds:

head: Component
What it does
Examples
rows: Single-phase induction motor
Windings in the fixed stator make a turning magnetic field that drags the rotor round. No brushes.
Water and pool pumps, fans, compressors, table saws
Universal (brush) motor
Runs on AC or DC. Carbon brushes feed current to the turning armature through a commutator. Fast and powerful for its size.
Drills, angle grinders, blenders, vacuum cleaners
Contactor
A heavy-duty switch closed by a coil, used to switch motors and other large loads.
Motor starters, air-conditioner compressors, pump panels
Relay
A small switch closed by a coil, used in control circuits.
Control panels, gate controllers, timers
Solenoid
A coil that pulls in an iron plunger when energised.
Water valves, door locks, vehicle starters
Overload relay
Trips the starter when the motor draws too much current for too long.
Every motor starter
Limit switch
A switch worked by a moving part when it reaches the end of its travel.
Sliding gates, garage doors, conveyors
Gearbox
A set of gears that lowers the speed and raises the turning force between a motor and its load.
Gate motors, mixers, conveyors

blocks.h: The parts of an induction motor

head: Part
What it is
rows: Stator
The fixed outer part: the frame, a core of steel laminations, and the windings in the slots of the core.
Laminations
Thin steel sheets, insulated from each other and stacked to make the core. They cut down the heating that a solid core would suffer.
Windings
Coils of enamelled copper wire. A single-phase motor has a **run (main) winding** and a **start (auxiliary) winding**.
Rotor
The turning part: aluminium or copper bars in a laminated core, called a squirrel cage, fixed on the shaft.
Air gap
The small, even space between the rotor and the stator, often only a fraction of a millimetre in small motors.
Shaft and key
The shaft carries the rotor. A key sits in a slot (the keyway) to lock a pulley or coupling to the shaft.
Bearings
Support the shaft so that it turns freely: ball bearings, or sleeve bushes in some small motors.
End shields (end bells)
The covers at each end that hold the bearings and keep the rotor centred in the stator.
Fan and fan cover
Blow air over the frame to cool the motor.
Terminal box
Where the supply leads and the winding leads are connected.
Centrifugal switch
In split-phase and capacitor-start motors: weights on the shaft fly out as it speeds up and open a switch that cuts out the start winding, usually at about 70–80% of full speed.
Capacitor
In capacitor motors: helps the start winding make a turning field. Marked in microfarads (µF) and volts.

head: Type
How it starts
Typical use
rows: Split-phase
A start winding of thinner wire, cut out by the centrifugal switch
Small machines, blowers and some bench grinders
Capacitor-start
A start winding with a start capacitor (often from about 70 µF to several hundred µF, in a black plastic case), both cut out by the centrifugal switch; strong starting
Pumps, compressors, table saws
Permanent split capacitor (PSC)
A smaller run capacitor (often 1–60 µF) stays connected all the time; no centrifugal switch
Ceiling and pedestal fans, air-conditioner fan motors, some pumps
Capacitor-start, capacitor-run
A start capacitor with a switch, and a run capacitor as well
Larger pumps and compressors
Shaded-pole
Copper shading rings on the poles; weak starting; no capacitor or switch
Small exhaust fans and some small desk fans

head: Marking
Meaning
rows: V
Rated voltage. Some motors are dual-voltage (for example 110/220 V) and are connected differently for each.
A or FLA
Full-load current: what the motor draws at its rated output.
kW or HP
Output power. 1 horsepower (HP) is about 0.75 kW.
rpm
Speed at full load, in revolutions per minute.
Hz
Supply frequency, in hertz.
Ph
Number of phases: 1 or 3.
Cap
Capacitor value in µF, and its voltage.
Ins. class
The highest temperature the insulation is built for (for example class B or F).
Duty
Continuous (S1 or 'Cont.') or for short periods only.

blocks.p: The magnetic field of a motor turns at a speed set by the supply frequency and the number of poles: **speed = 120 × frequency ÷ poles**. On 50 Hz, a 2-pole motor's field turns at 3000 rpm and a 4-pole motor's at 1500 rpm. The rotor of an induction motor always turns a little slower than its field (this is called slip), so the nameplates read about 2850 rpm and 1440 rpm.

blocks.note: Many motors in Jamaica come from the US and are made for 60 Hz. On JPS's 50 Hz supply they run about one-sixth slower, so pumps and fans deliver less, and unless the nameplate says 50/60 Hz they may run hotter. Copy the frequency from the nameplate and check it when a motor is replaced.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: In a universal motor, current flows through the field windings and then, through two **carbon brushes**, into the **armature**. The brushes press on the **commutator**, a ring of copper bars on the armature, held by springs. As the armature turns the brushes wear down, and the commutator gets a thin, even brown film. Worn brushes, a dirty or damaged commutator, or weak springs cause sparking and loss of power.
Before you loosen a single screw, the component must be disconnected from every source of energy: electrical, stored and mechanical.

head: Equipment
How to make it safe
rows: Plug-in (bench grinder, drill, pedestal fan)
Unplug it and keep the plug in view on the bench.
Fixed (pump, air-conditioner, machine on an isolator)

Isolate, lock off with your own padlock, tag, and prove dead at the motor terminals between every pair of conductors and each conductor to earth, with a tester proved before and after. Your supervisor leads this on site.
Battery tool
Take the battery pack off.
Control panel (contactors, relays)
Isolate both the power supply and any separate control supply, then lock off and prove dead.

blocks.note: Many pumps start by themselves from a float switch, pressure switch or timer, and many compressors from a pressure switch. A motor that is standing still may start at any moment. Never rely on the control switch: isolate and lock off.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Stored energy
The danger
How to control it
rows: Capacitors
A shock after the supply is off
Discharge with the Centre's resistor discharge tool, as the instructor shows, then check with a meter that no voltage is left. Never short the terminals with a screwdriver.
Springs (contactors, relays, brush holders, centrifugal switches)
Parts fly out and hit your eyes
Wear safety glasses; hold the part and release springs slowly, covering them with your hand or a cloth.
Belts and pulleys
Fingers trapped in nip points
Take belts off only with the machine isolated and stopped.
Heavy parts (rotors, motors, gearboxes)
Parts fall and crush hands or feet
Support them; lift with two people or a lifting aid.
Pressure (pumps and compressors)
Water or air blasts out
Release the pressure and drain before you open anything.
Heat
Burns from a motor that has just run
Let it cool before you handle it.

head: Hazard
How to control it
rows: Manual handling

Small motors weigh from a few kilograms to 40 kg or more. A common guide is that one person should not lift much more than about 20–25 kg, and less if the load is awkward. Use two people or a lifting aid, and keep your back straight.
Sharp edges
Laminations, fan blades and sheet-metal covers can cut. Wear gloves where it is safe to do so.
Cleaning solvents
Fumes and fire: use them in a ventilated place, with gloves, away from flames and hot work.
Compressed air
Blows dust and grit into eyes: use low pressure, wear eye protection, and never point it at anyone or at your skin.
Carbon and winding dust
Wear a dust mask when cleaning brush motors.
Hammering
Flying chips and damaged parts: use pullers and a soft-faced mallet, never a steel hammer on shafts, bearings or castings.
Pinch points
Fingers between the rotor and stator, or under end shields: keep fingers clear as parts come together.

blocks.note: Before you start, check your PPE: safety glasses, safety boots and suitable gloves. Remove rings and watches, and tie back long hair.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A motor that has been taken apart carelessly may go back together with the leads in the wrong place, a washer missing or a bearing damaged. Ten minutes of planning and recording saves hours later.

ul: Read the maker's **service manual**. It gives the order for taking the component apart, the tightening torques and the parts numbers.
Study the **exploded diagram**: a drawing that shows the parts spread apart, in the order they fit together, each with a number from the parts list.
Collect the tools before you start, and set out a clean, well-lit bench with **labelled trays** and a job card.
If there is no manual, ask your instructor and record everything as you go.

blocks.h: Record before you take it apart

flow: Copy the nameplate onto the job card
Photograph the terminal box and every connection
Label each lead (numbered tags or marked tape) and draw a sketch
Make match marks across each end-shield joint: for example one punch dot at the drive end and two at the other end
As each part comes off, put it in a tray in order, and note shims, spacers, wave washers and which way parts face
Write down any damage you find

blocks.note: When screws of different lengths come out of one case (as in many drills and grinders), push them through a piece of card in the same pattern as the holes. Each one then goes back where it came from.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Tool
Use
Take care
rows: Spanners and sockets
Nuts and bolts
Use the exact size, metric or imperial, so that you do not round the corners.
Hex (Allen) keys
Grub screws and socket cap screws
Push the key fully into the socket before you turn it.
Circlip pliers
Removing and fitting circlips
External pliers open when squeezed (for clips on a shaft); internal pliers close when squeezed (for clips in a bore). Wear safety glasses.
Gear (pulley) puller, two- or three-jaw
Pulling pulleys, gears, couplings and bearings off shafts
Centre the screw on the shaft end, keep the jaws square, and turn steadily.
Bearing separator
Gets behind a bearing so that the puller pulls on the inner race
Close it evenly round the bearing.
Soft-faced mallet (rubber, nylon or copper)
Loosening end shields and tapping parts into place
Tap evenly round the edge; never a steel hammer on parts.
Brass or aluminium drift
Tapping out keys and pins
A soft drift will not mark the steel.
Arbor press
Pressing bearings and bushes on and off steadily
Support the part properly; press only on the correct ring of a bearing.
Induction bearing heater
Heating bearings so that they slide onto the shaft
Set the temperature the maker gives; never use a flame.
Torque wrench
Tightening bolts and terminals to the maker's value
Set it to the stated torque and return it to its lowest setting after use.
Feeler gauges
Measuring small gaps
Keep them clean and unbent.
Centre punch or marker
Match marks
Mark where the marks will not be machined or painted over.
Multimeter and insulation resistance tester
Winding, coil, contact and insulation tests
Check them before use.

blocks.p: Most threads are **right-hand**: they tighten clockwise and loosen **anticlockwise**. Some parts have **left-hand** threads, so that the turning of the machine tightens them instead of loosening them: for example the nut on the left-hand wheel of a bench grinder, and some fan-blade nuts. They may be marked 'LH' or with notches. If a nut will not move, check which way it turns before you use more force.
This is the usual order for a small single-phase induction motor. Always follow the maker's manual where there is one.

flow: Make it safe: unplug or isolate, lock off and prove dead; discharge the capacitor
Record: nameplate, photos, labels on every lead; then disconnect the leads
Slacken and remove the belt, undo the mounting bolts and lift the motor to a clean bench, with help if it is heavy
Remove the pulley or coupling: undo the grub screw, then use a puller; keep the key
Remove the fan cover, then the fan
Make match marks across both end-shield joints
Undo the end-shield bolts and put them in a labelled tray
Loosen the end shield at the end away from the shaft extension by tapping evenly round its edge with a soft-faced mallet
Draw the rotor out with the other end shield, keeping it straight and supporting its weight so that it does not drag on the windings
Lay the rotor on a clean, soft surface
Remove the bearings only if they are to be replaced

ul: Slacken the belt first, then undo the grub screw with the right hex key.
Fit the puller jaws behind the pulley hub, not on the thin rim, which can crack, especially on a cast pulley.
Centre the puller screw on the shaft end (use a shaft protector if there is one) and turn it steadily.
Keep the key: tap it out with a soft drift if it stays in the keyway.
Never hammer a pulley off. The shock passes along the shaft into the bearings and can crack the pulley or the end shield.

blocks.p: The air gap is very small, so a rotor that tilts or drops scrapes the stator and can tear the winding insulation. Hold the shaft and support the rotor's weight with both hands as it comes out, keeping it level and straight. On a heavy rotor, use a second person. Never hold it by the fan or by the windings' leads.

ul: On many tools the brushes can be reached through caps on the sides. On others the case must be opened.
Note which way each brush sits before you remove it. If old brushes are to go back, they must go back the same way, because they wear to the curve of the commutator.
Note the order of gears and washers in the gearbox, and which wires go to the switch and the field, before you lift the armature out.
Some brushes have a built-in cut-off pin that stops the motor when the brush is worn. Replace them with the same type.

blocks.note: Never lever an end shield off with a screwdriver against the windings, and never hit a shaft end with a steel hammer. If a part will not come off, stop and ask: there may be a hidden screw, circlip or pin.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Clean the parts first so that you can see them clearly, then inspect each one and write what you find on the job card.

head: Method
Use it for
Take care
rows: Soft brush and lint-free cloth
Dust on windings and frames
Do not scrape the winding insulation.
Dry compressed air at low pressure
Blowing dust out of windings and vents
Use low pressure (often no more than about 2 bar, 30 psi; follow the Centre's rule), wear eye protection and keep others clear.
Vacuum cleaner
Carbon dust in brush motors
Collects the dust instead of spreading it.
Approved degreaser on a cloth
Grease on end shields, shafts and frames
Ventilation, gloves, no flames. Never soak windings, and never use petrol.
Commutator stone or the maker's fine abrasive
Light dirt on a commutator
Never emery cloth: it leaves conductive grit between the bars.

head: Part
Look for
What it means
rows: Bearings
Roughness, noise or play when turned by hand; blue or brown marks; rust
Worn, overheated or wet: replace
Shaft
Scoring, a bent shaft, worn bearing seats, a damaged keyway or thread
Report it: the shaft may need repair
Rotor
A bright rubbed band on one side
Worn bearings or a bent shaft let it rub the stator
Stator windings
Dark or burnt insulation, a burnt smell, broken leads, loose ties, oil or dirt
Overheating: find the cause; a burnt winding needs a specialist rewind
Centrifugal switch
Burnt contacts; weights or springs that are stiff, worn or broken
The start winding may not cut in or out: repair or replace as the maker says
Capacitor
Bulging, leaking, cracks, a burnt smell; its value on a capacitance meter
Replace with the same µF, the same or a higher voltage, and the same type (start or run)
Carbon brushes
Length below the maker's limit; chips, cracks or uneven wear; weak springs; sticking in the holder
Replace both brushes together with the maker's type
Commutator
Normal: smooth, with an even chocolate-brown film. Faults: deep grooves, burnt or raised bars, pitting
Clean light dirt; a badly worn commutator needs a specialist
End shields
Cracks; a bearing loose in its housing
Replace the end shield
Fan, cover and terminal box
Broken blades, cracks, burnt terminals, cracked lead insulation
Replace damaged parts

blocks.note: Burnt windings are a result, not a cause. Look for why the motor overheated: an overload, blocked cooling, failed bearings, a start winding that stayed in circuit (capacitor or centrifugal switch fault), low voltage, or a 60 Hz motor working hard on 50 Hz. Otherwise the rewound motor will burn out again.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Test
How
A good result
rows: Winding continuity and resistance
Ohmmeter across each winding
A low reading (often a few ohms on a small motor); the start winding usually reads higher than the run winding. OL means a broken winding.
Insulation resistance
500 V DC between the windings (joined together) and the frame
High: at least the Centre's pass figure, often 1 MΩ; a good motor usually reads far more. A low reading means damp, dirt or damaged insulation.
Capacitor value
Capacitance range, after discharging
Within the tolerance printed on it
Armature of a brush motor
Resistance between each pair of neighbouring commutator bars
All about the same; one much higher or lower reading shows a faulty coil

blocks.p: Most small motors run on ball bearings. Some fans and small motors use **sleeve bearings** (bushes) of porous bronze soaked in oil instead. Bearing trouble is the most common reason for taking a motor apart.

Take the example **6203-2RS**. The **6** means a deep-groove ball bearing. The **2** is the series (a light bearing). The **03** is the bore code: 00 = 10 mm, 01 = 12 mm, 02 = 15 mm, 03 = 17 mm, and from 04 upwards multiply by 5 (04 = 20 mm, 05 = 25 mm). A 6303 has the same 17 mm bore but is a heavier bearing with a bigger outside diameter.

head: Suffix
Meaning
Lubrication
rows: 2RS (other makers use similar codes)
Two rubber seals: keep out dust and water
Greased for life by the maker; do not add grease and do not wash it
ZZ (or 2Z)
Two metal shields: keep out larger dirt, but not water
Greased for life by the maker
No suffix
Open bearing
Greased as the maker says, usually about one-third to one-half full; too much grease makes it run hot

blocks.note: Replace a bearing with one of the **same number and suffix**, or an equivalent the maker approves. On a pump, an outdoor fan or anything near water, the seals matter as much as the size.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Support the shaft and protect its end
Fit a puller, or a bearing separator and puller, so that it pulls on the inner race (the ring that grips the shaft)
Turn the screw slowly and evenly, keeping the puller square
Clean the shaft and check the bearing seat for scoring and wear

blocks.p: If you pull on the outer race, the force passes through the balls and dents the tracks. A bearing removed that way is scrap. In practice, a bearing that has been pulled off is usually not used again.

ul: Keep it clean, in its packet, until you need it. Dirt shortens its life.
Check that the shaft seat is clean, smooth and free of burrs.

Press only on the ring that has the tight fit: the **inner race** when fitting onto a shaft, the **outer race** when fitting into a housing. Use a press or a clean tube that bears on that ring only, and push it on square until it meets the shoulder.
Never hammer a bearing, and never press on the seals, the shields or the wrong race.

Or heat the bearing with an **induction bearing heater** to the temperature the maker gives (open bearings are often heated to about 110 °C; sealed and shielded bearings need less, often about 80 °C). The inner ring grows, slides on, and grips as it cools. Never use a flame, and never cool it in water.
After fitting, it should turn smoothly and quietly.

blocks.note: **Force must never pass through the balls.** Every fitting and removal method is about making sure of that.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Sign
Likely cause
rows: Rough or grinding noise
Wear, or dirt inside the bearing
Squealing
Lack of grease, or misalignment
Blue or brown marks on the races
Overheating: too much or too little grease, a tight belt or an overload
Rust
Water getting in: pumps, outdoor motors and salt air
Polished, scored shaft under the bearing
The inner race was turning on the shaft (the bearing seat is worn)
Bearing loose in the end shield
A worn housing
Early failure at the pulley end
A belt that is too tight, or a pulley that is out of line

blocks.p: A **contactor** is a switch closed by a magnet. When its coil is energised, the fixed iron core becomes a magnet and pulls in the moving **armature**, which carries the moving contacts onto the fixed contacts. When the coil is switched off, springs push the armature away and the contacts open.

head: Part
What it does
rows: Coil
Makes the magnetic pull when energised; marked with its voltage, such as 24 V, 110 V or 220 V AC
Fixed core (magnet)
Laminated iron that the coil magnetises
Armature
The moving iron part that is pulled in, carrying the moving contacts
Shading ring
A copper ring set into the face of an AC magnet; it keeps some pull while the AC passes through zero, so the armature does not chatter
Main contacts
Silver-alloy contacts that switch the load current
Auxiliary contacts
Small contacts for the control circuit: normally open (NO) or normally closed (NC)
Springs
Push the armature open and give the contacts their pressure
Arc chutes or shields
Contain and cool the arc as the contacts open

blocks.h: Relays, solenoids, overloads and limit switches

ul: A **relay** is a small contactor for control circuits. Many plug into a base (8-pin, 11-pin or 14-pin). Each set of contacts has a common (COM), a normally open (NO) and a normally closed (NC) terminal.
A **solenoid** is a coil that pulls in an iron plunger when it is energised; a spring returns the plunger. Water valves, door locks and vehicle starters use them.

A **thermal overload relay** carries the motor current through heaters beside bimetal strips. If the current is too high for too long, the strips bend and open a contact in the coil circuit, which drops out the contactor. It is set to the motor's full-load current from the nameplate.
A **DOL (direct-on-line) starter** is a contactor, an overload relay and start and stop buttons: it switches the motor straight onto the full supply.
A **limit switch** is worked by a lever, roller or plunger when a moving part reaches the end of its travel, for example to stop a sliding gate.

flow: Isolate the panel, including any separate control supply; lock off, tag and prove dead
Label and photograph every wire, then remove the contactor
On the bench, read the maker's instructions
Remove the cover or arc chute and note how the parts sit
Wearing safety glasses, take out the moving contacts, springs, armature and coil, holding the springs as they are released
Put the parts in a tray in the order they came out

head: Part
Good
Faulty, and what to do
rows: Main contacts
Dull grey or darkened, but smooth and thick
Deep pits, heavy wear to the maker's limit, or welded: fit the maker's contact kit, all contacts as a set. Never file or use emery: it removes the silver.
Magnet faces
Clean, flat, no rust
Dirt, rust or grease stop the faces meeting and cause humming: clean them as the maker says
Shading ring
Whole and firmly seated
Cracked or missing: loud chatter and heat; replace the magnet or the contactor
Coil
No burnt smell or marks; resistance close to the maker's or a known good coil's
OL: open coil; much lower than normal: shorted turns. Replace it.
Springs
Unbroken, springy
Broken or weak: replace with the maker's springs
Moving parts
Move freely by hand and return fully
Sticking: clean and check for damage

ul: Press the armature in by hand: it should move freely and spring back fully.
Check each contact with the ohmmeter. A **normally open** contact reads **OL** at rest and near **0 Ω** with the armature pressed in. A **normally closed** contact does the opposite.
Measure and record the coil resistance.
Refit and reconnect the contactor exactly as recorded.

blocks.note: Contactor and relay springs are small and strong. Wear safety glasses, release them slowly under your thumb or a cloth, and count them into the tray: a spring lost on the floor means the contactor cannot be rebuilt.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Reassemble in the **reverse order** of dismantling, using your notes, photos and match marks. Make sure every part is clean and every new part is the right one before you start.

flow: Fit the bearings to the shaft, pressing on the inner race only
Put any wave washer, shim or spacer back where your notes say
Guide the rotor into the stator, keeping it straight so that it does not touch the windings
Fit the end shields with the match marks lined up, and put the bolts in finger-tight
Tighten the bolts a little at a time in a criss-cross order, turning the shaft by hand as you go
Check that the shaft turns freely and has a little end float
Refit the fan, the fan cover, the key and the pulley
Reconnect the leads as recorded and tighten the terminals to the maker's torque
Check that the parts tray is empty, then do the tests

ul: The shaft turns freely and quietly by hand, with no rubbing or tight spots.
There is a little end float (end-to-end movement), but not a lot. The wave washer takes up most of it.
No lead is trapped under an end shield or a cover. A trapped lead can cut through and cause an earth fault.
Nothing is left over in the tray. A part left over means something was missed: find out where it goes.

blocks.h: Tests before the motor goes back

head: Test
How
A good result
rows: Turn by hand
Turn the shaft slowly through several turns
Free and quiet
Winding continuity
Ohmmeter across each winding
The same readings as before dismantling, or the maker's
Insulation resistance
500 V DC from the windings to the frame
At least the Centre's pass figure, often 1 MΩ
Earth continuity
From the frame to the earth terminal or the plug's earth pin
A very low reading
Run test
By the instructor or a competent person, on the protected test bench
Correct direction, no unusual noise or vibration, current not above the nameplate figure, and on capacitor-start motors a click as the centrifugal switch opens

ul: A **single-phase induction motor** is reversed by swapping the start (auxiliary) winding's leads compared with the run winding, as the connection diagram shows. Swapping the line and neutral at the plug does **not** reverse it.
A **three-phase motor** is reversed by swapping any two supply lines.
A **universal motor** is reversed by swapping the armature (brush) leads compared with the field.
If a motor runs the wrong way after a repair, the leads were probably reconnected wrongly: check them against your photos.

head: Symptom
Likely cause
rows: Shaft stiff or rubbing after the bolts are tightened
End shields drawn up unevenly or off their match marks; a bearing not fully seated; dirt in a housing
Hums but will not start
Start circuit fault: capacitor, centrifugal switch or a start-winding lead; or a seized bearing
Runs the wrong way
Start-winding leads swapped
Noisy or vibrating
A bearing damaged when it was fitted; the fan rubbing its cover; a loose pulley; a bent shaft
Overheats
Wrong connection on a dual-voltage motor; start winding not cutting out; belt too tight; fan or vents blocked
Trips the breaker or GFCI
An earth fault, often a lead trapped under an end shield

ul: Refit every guard and cover before the equipment goes back into use.
Complete the job card: nameplate details, faults found, parts replaced (bearing numbers, brush type, capacitor value), test results, and who did and checked the work.
Put old bearings and brushes in the scrap-metal or waste bin the Centre uses, old capacitors and boards in e-waste, and oily or solvent-soaked rags in a closed metal bin, because they can catch fire.
Clean the bench and return the tools.

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can name the parts of a single-phase induction motor and a brush motor, and say what each does.
I can tell split-phase, capacitor-start, PSC and shaded-pole motors apart.
I can read a motor nameplate, and explain rpm, Hz, µF and full-load current.
I can make a motor or contactor safe, including capacitors, springs, belts, pressure and heavy parts.
I can plan a job from the service manual and exploded diagram.
I can record the wiring, make match marks and keep parts in order.
I can choose and use pullers, circlip pliers, hex keys, a soft-faced mallet, a press and a torque wrench.
I can remove a pulley and draw out a rotor without damage.
I can clean motor parts safely and say what must never be used.
I can inspect bearings, shafts, windings, centrifugal switches, capacitors, brushes and commutators and judge what needs replacing.
I can read a bearing number and choose the right replacement.
I can remove and fit a bearing without passing force through the balls.
I can take apart, inspect and test a contactor and a relay.
I can reassemble a motor in the right order, tightening evenly and checking that it turns freely.
I can carry out the dead tests and say who does the run test.
I can explain how to reverse single-phase, three-phase and universal motors.
I can complete the job card and dispose of waste correctly.

terms: Air gap
The small space between the rotor and the stator.
Arbor press
A bench press for pushing bearings and bushes on and off steadily.
Armature
The moving iron part of a contactor or relay; also the turning part of a brush motor.
Centrifugal switch
A switch on the shaft that cuts out the start winding as the motor reaches speed.
Circlip
A spring clip in a groove that holds a part on a shaft or in a bore.
Commutator
The ring of copper bars on a brush motor's armature, on which the brushes run.
Contactor
A heavy-duty switch closed by a coil, used for motors and large loads.
End float
The small end-to-end movement of a motor shaft.
End shield (end bell)
The cover at each end of a motor that holds a bearing.
Exploded diagram
A drawing that shows how the parts fit together, spread apart in order.
Inner race
The ring of a bearing that fits on the shaft.
Key
A small metal piece in a slot that locks a pulley or coupling to its shaft.
Laminations
Thin, insulated steel sheets stacked to make a motor core.
Match marks
Marks made across a joint before dismantling so that the parts go back in the same position.
Nameplate
The plate on a motor that gives its voltage, current, power, speed and frequency.
Overload relay
A device that trips a motor starter when the motor draws too much current for too long.
Puller
A tool with jaws and a centre screw for drawing pulleys, gears and bearings off shafts.
Rotor
The turning part of an induction motor.
Shading ring
A copper ring on an AC magnet face that stops the armature chattering.
Solenoid
A coil that pulls in an iron plunger when energised.
Stator
The fixed part of a motor, holding the windings.

c1.title: A table saw motor in Santa Cruz
c1.text: Trainee Rohan and Mr Everton Spence, a maintenance electrician, are to take the motor off a table saw at a furniture workshop in Santa Cruz, St Elizabeth, and replace its bearings. The 220 V capacitor-start motor is wired through flexible conduit to a lockable isolator. It drives the saw by a V-belt, and its pulley is held by a key and a grub screw. The nameplate gives 1.5 kW, 1440 rpm, 50 Hz. The operator says that for some weeks the motor has sometimes hummed at switch-on without turning, until he switched off and tried again.

c2.title: A hammer drill that sparks
c2.text: At a tool-hire shop in Ocho Rios, St Ann, trainee Danielle is given a 110 V hammer drill that sparks heavily at its vents and has lost power. Its plastic case is marked with a square inside a square. The maker's manual says that the carbon brushes must be replaced when they are worn to 6 mm. Danielle unplugs the drill and keeps the plug on the bench.

c3.title: Noisy bearings on a hotel pool pump
c3.text: At a hotel in Negril, Westmoreland, the motor of a pool pump has become noisy. The maintenance team has isolated it, locked it off and taken it to the workshop. Trainee Andre finds that the drive-end bearing feels rough when he turns it by hand. It is marked 6203-2RS. The hotel's store has bearings marked 6203-ZZ, 6203-2RS, 6303-2RS and 6204-2RS, and the workshop has an induction bearing heater.

c4.title: A chattering contactor at a Port Maria bakery
c4.text: The dough mixer at a bakery in Port Maria, St Mary, is started by a contactor with a 220 V AC coil. The contactor has started to chatter and hum loudly. The panel has been isolated, locked off and proved dead, and trainee Keisha is given the contactor on the bench, with the maker's instructions and a contact kit.

c5.title: Rebuilding a compressor motor in Falmouth
c5.text: At the Centre in Falmouth, Trelawny, trainees Kemar and Shanelle have stripped and rebuilt the 110 V capacitor-start motor of a small air compressor. After tightening the end-shield bolts, they find the shaft stiff, with a light rub at one point. When that has been put right, they measure the start winding at 4.2 Ω and the run winding at 1.8 Ω. One flat washer is still in the parts tray.

questions.q: The motor is isolated, locked off and proved dead. What is the right order for getting the pulley off?
o: Use the puller first, and undo the grub screw once it moves
Pull the pulley with the puller while the belt is tight
Knock the pulley off with a steel hammer, then the key
Slacken the belt, undo the grub screw, then use a puller
questions.why: The belt must be slack so that it can come off, and the grub screw must be out, or the puller fights it and can damage the shaft. A puller pushes steadily on the shaft centre; hammering sends shocks into the bearings and can crack a cast pulley.

questions.q: What does '1440 rpm' on the nameplate tell Rohan?
o: The motor takes 1440 W from the supply when it is running
The shaft turns about 1440 times a minute at full load
Each winding should read about 1440 Ω when tested
The motor needs servicing every 1440 hours of use
questions.why: rpm means revolutions per minute. On 50 Hz a four-pole motor's field turns at 1500 rpm, and an induction motor runs a little slower than its field, here 1440 rpm at full load. The power is given separately, in kW (here 1.5 kW).

questions.q: Behind one bearing Rohan finds a thin, wavy spring washer. What should he do?
o: Fit it at whichever end is easier when rebuilding
Throw it away, as it is only loose packing material
Note which end it came from and refit it there
Flatten it in the vice so the shaft has no end float
questions.why: A wave washer presses lightly on one bearing's outer race, taking up end float and keeping the bearings quiet. It belongs at one end only. Record its position, like every shim and spacer, and put it back where it came from.

questions.q: Given the operator's report, which parts should Rohan check most carefully while the motor is apart?
o: The pulley key and the grub screw that holds it
The fan cover and the tension of the V-belt
The start capacitor and centrifugal switch
The frame's paint and the fixing of the nameplate
questions.why: A capacitor-start motor that hums without turning is usually not getting its start winding into circuit: a failing start capacitor, centrifugal switch contacts that do not close, or a broken start-winding lead. Check them now, or the hum will come back after the new bearings are fitted.

questions.q: One brush measures 5 mm and the other 9 mm. What should Danielle do?
o: Swap the two brushes round to even out the wear
Replace both with the maker's brushes
Stretch the springs so the old brushes press harder
Replace only the 5 mm brush, as the other is fine
questions.why: One brush is below the 6 mm limit, so the brushes must be changed. They are replaced as a pair, with the maker's type, so that both bed in together and wear evenly. Stretched springs or swapped brushes do not cure worn brushes and can damage the commutator.

questions.q: The commutator has an even chocolate-brown colour, but a few bars are burnt and there are deep grooves. What does this mean?
o: The brown film is normal; the burnt, grooved bars are not
The brown film is a fault, so it must be filed off the bars
The grooves are normal, but the brown colour is a fault
All of it is normal wear and needs no attention
questions.why: A smooth chocolate-brown film forms on a healthy commutator and helps the brushes run well. Burnt bars and deep grooves cause heavy sparking and loss of power; they need specialist repair (skimming, or a new armature), as the maker and instructor advise.

questions.q: What should Danielle use to clean light dirt off the commutator?
o: A commutator stone, as the maker says
A wire brush, as it gets into the slots
Petrol, as it dissolves the carbon dust
Emery cloth, as it cuts the dirt quickly
questions.why: Emery cloth leaves hard, conductive grit between the bars, a wire brush scratches the copper, and petrol is a fire risk. Use a commutator stone or the fine abrasive the maker states, as the instructor shows, then clean away the dust.

questions.q: The drill is double insulated. Which test should follow the repair, before the instructor's run test?
o: Resistance of the new brushes on the ohms range
Earth continuity from the earth pin to the metal chuck
Insulation resistance, plug pins to the metal chuck
Current drawn while Danielle runs it on her own bench
questions.why: A double-insulated tool has a two-pin plug and no earth conductor, so there is no earth path to test. Its safety depends on its insulation, so test from the joined plug pins to metal you can touch, such as the chuck. Running it is for the instructor on the protected bench.

questions.q: Which bearing should Andre fit?
questions.why: Fit the same number with the same seals. 2RS means two rubber seals, which keep out water and dust, which matters on a pool pump; ZZ has metal shields that are not water-tight. 6303 is a heavier bearing with a bigger outside, and 6204 has a 20 mm bore instead of 17 mm.

questions.q: How should Andre use the bearing heater to fit the new bearing?
o: Heat it to the maker's temperature, then slide it on
Heat it, then cool it in water just before fitting
Heat the shaft instead, so that the shaft expands
Heat it until it glows red, so that it slides on easily
questions.why: Heat makes the inner ring grow so that it slides onto the shaft, then grips as it cools. Too much heat ruins the steel, the grease and the seals (sealed bearings have a lower limit), heating the shaft makes the fit tighter, and water would shrink the bearing before it is on.

questions.q: Under the old bearing, the shaft is polished and scored all the way round. What does this suggest?
o: The motor was run in the wrong direction
The rotor was rubbing on the stator core
The inner race was turning on the shaft
The bearing had too much grease in it
questions.why: The inner race should be a tight fit and turn with the shaft. When it slips, it polishes and wears the bearing seat, and the new bearing may then be loose too. Report it: the shaft may need repair before the motor goes back.

questions.q: The rotor has a bright rubbed band on one side, with matching marks in the stator bore. What is the most likely cause?
o: The windings were cleaned with dry, low-pressure air
The motor was run with too little load
Worn bearings let the rotor sag and rub
The fan was fitted the wrong way round
questions.why: The air gap between rotor and stator is only a fraction of a millimetre. When the bearings wear, the rotor drops and rubs, which damages the core and can damage the windings. Look for this whenever you replace worn bearings, and report it.

questions.q: Keisha finds the main contacts dark grey, but still thick and smooth. What should she do with them?
o: Leave them; dark grey is normal for them
Coat them with grease so they do not burn
File them bright, so that they conduct better
Rub them with emery cloth until they shine
questions.why: Contactor contacts are a silver alloy that darkens in normal use and still conducts well. Filing or emery removes the silver and leaves grit, and grease collects dirt and burns. Fit the maker's contact kit only when the contacts are badly pitted or worn to the maker's limit.

questions.q: She finds a cracked copper ring set into one face of the fixed magnet, and dirt on the magnet faces. What is the most likely cause of the chatter?
o: The springs that push the armature open
The dark grey colour of the main contacts
Coil terminals that have been tightened fully
The cracked shading ring on the magnet face
questions.why: On an AC coil the magnetic pull falls to zero 100 times a second. The shading ring keeps some pull during those moments; when it cracks, or dirt stops the faces meeting, the armature buzzes and chatters. Clean the faces, and replace the magnet or the contactor as the maker says.

questions.q: After reassembly, Keisha checks a normally open (NO) auxiliary contact with the ohmmeter. What should she read?
o: Near 0 Ω both at rest and with the armature pressed in
OL at rest, and near 0 Ω with the armature pressed in
Near 0 Ω at rest, and OL with the armature pressed in
OL both at rest and with the armature pressed in
questions.why: A normally open contact is open (OL) when the coil is not energised and closes (near 0 Ω) when the armature is pulled, or pushed, in. A normally closed contact does the opposite. A reading that does not change means a stuck, worn or wrongly assembled contact.

questions.q: What is the most likely reason the shaft became stiff when the bolts were tightened?
o: The end shields were drawn up unevenly
The winding leads were swapped in the box
The capacitor was not discharged first
The new bearings are too new to turn freely
questions.why: End-shield bolts are tightened a little at a time in a criss-cross order, turning the shaft by hand as you go. Pulling one side up first tilts the shield, so the bearings bind and the rotor can touch the stator. Slacken, line up the match marks and tighten evenly.

questions.q: What do the readings of 4.2 Ω and 1.8 Ω show?
o: The start winding is faulty, as it should match the run winding
Both windings are whole; the start winding usually reads higher
The run winding is open, because its reading is lower
Both windings are shorted, since good windings read OL
questions.why: A low reading shows that a winding is continuous; OL would mean a break. The start winding is wound with thinner wire, so it usually reads higher than the run winding. Compare with the maker's figures, or a good motor of the same type, when you can.

questions.q: What should Kemar and Shanelle do about the washer left in the tray?
o: Keep it in the tray, ready for the next motor job
Throw it away, since the motor is already together
Run the motor to hear whether anything is loose
Find where it came from, using notes and photos
questions.why: A part left over means something was missed. A missing washer can let the shaft move, a cover rattle or a terminal work loose. Check the notes, photos and exploded diagram, and refit it before the tests.

questions.q: When the instructor runs the motor, it turns the wrong way for the compressor. What is the usual cure on this motor?
o: Fit the capacitor the other way round
Turn the rotor round, end for end, in the stator
Swap the line and neutral at the plug
Swap the start winding leads at the terminals
questions.why: A capacitor-start motor's direction is set by how the start winding is connected compared with the run winding. Swapping line and neutral changes both together, so the direction stays the same, and a motor capacitor is not polarised. Check the connections against the photos and the connection diagram.

questions.q: The nut on the left-hand wheel of a bench grinder will not loosen when it is turned anticlockwise. What is the most likely reason?
o: It is seized, so it needs a much longer spanner
It has a left-hand thread, so it loosens clockwise
It is a metric nut that was put on an imperial thread
It must be heated with a gas torch before it moves
questions.why: The nut on the left-hand wheel of a bench grinder normally has a left-hand thread, so that the turning wheel tightens it instead of loosening it. Turn it clockwise to loosen it. Look for an 'LH' mark before you force any nut.
